title: Book 6, Chapter 18 — Seventeenth Year of the War—The Sicilian Campaign—Affair of the Hermae—Departure of the Expedition
paragraphs: The same winter the Athenians resolved to sail again to Sicily, with a larger force than the one under Laches and Eurymedon, and, if possible, to conquer the island. Most of them were ignorant of its size and of the number of its inhabitants, Hellenic and barbarian, and of the fact that they were taking on a war not much smaller than the one against the Peloponnesians. The voyage round Sicily in a merchantman is not far short of eight days; and yet, large as the island is, only two miles of sea keep it from being mainland.

It was originally settled as follows, and these are the peoples who occupied it. The earliest inhabitants spoken of in any part of the country are the Cyclopes and the Laestrygones; but I cannot say what race they were, where they came from, or where they went, and must leave my readers to what the poets have said of them and to what is generally known. The Sicanians appear to have been the next settlers, although they pretend to have been the first of all and aboriginal; but the facts show that they were Iberians, driven by the Ligurians from the river Sicanus in Iberia. It is from them that the island, formerly called Trinacria, took its name of Sicania, and to this day they inhabit the western part of Sicily. On the fall of Ilium some of the Trojans escaped from the Achaeans, came to Sicily by ship, and settled next to the Sicanians under the general name of Elymi; their towns being called Eryx and Egesta. With them settled some Phocians, carried on their way from Troy by a storm, first to Libya and from there to Sicily. The Sicels crossed over to Sicily from their first home in Italy, fleeing from the Opicans, as tradition says and as seems likely enough, on rafts, having watched until the wind set down the strait so they could make the crossing — though perhaps they may have sailed over by some other means. Even today there are still Sicels in Italy; and the country took its name of Italy from Italus, a king of the Sicels, so called. They came over to Sicily with a great host, defeated the Sicanians in battle, and forced them to move to the south and west of the island, which thus came to be called Sicily instead of Sicania. After they crossed over they continued to enjoy the richest parts of the country for almost three hundred years before any Hellenes came to Sicily; indeed they still hold the centre and north of the island. There were also Phoenicians living all round Sicily, who had occupied promontories on the coasts and the islets next to them in order to trade with the Sicels. But when the Hellenes began to arrive in considerable numbers by sea, the Phoenicians abandoned most of their stations and concentrated themselves at Motye, Soloeis, and Panormus, near the Elymi — partly because they trusted in their alliance, and also because these are the nearest points for the voyage between Carthage and Sicily.

These were the barbarians in Sicily, settled as I have said. Of the Hellenes, the first to arrive were Chalcidians from Euboea with Thucles, their founder. They founded Naxos and built the altar to Apollo Archegetes, which now stands outside the town and on which the deputies for the games sacrifice before sailing from Sicily. Syracuse was founded the year afterwards by Archias, one of the Heraclids from Corinth, who began by driving out the Sicels from the island on which the inner city now stands, though it is no longer surrounded by water; in time the outer town also was taken within the walls and became populous. Meanwhile Thucles and the Chalcidians set out from Naxos in the fifth year after the founding of Syracuse, drove out the Sicels by force of arms, and founded Leontini and afterwards Catana; the Catanians themselves choosing Evarchus as their founder.

About the same time Lamis arrived in Sicily with a colony from Megara. After founding a place called Trotilus beyond the river Pantacyas, then leaving it and for a short time joining the Chalcidians at Leontini, he was driven out by them and founded Thapsus. After his death his companions were driven out of Thapsus and founded a place called Hyblaean Megara; Hyblon, a Sicel king, having given up the place and inviting them there. They lived there two hundred and forty-five years, after which they were expelled from the city and the country by the Syracusan tyrant Gelo. Before their expulsion, however, a hundred years after settling there, they had sent out Pamillus and founded Selinus; he had come from their mother country Megara to join them in its founding. Gela was founded by Antiphemus from Rhodes and Entimus from Crete, who jointly led a colony there, in the forty-fifth year after the founding of Syracuse. The town took its name from the river Gelas, the place where the citadel now stands and which was first fortified being called Lindii. The institutions they adopted were Dorian. Almost a hundred and eight years after the founding of Gela, the Geloans founded Acragas (Agrigentum), so called from the river of that name, making Aristonous and Pystilus their founders, and giving the colony their own institutions. Zancle was originally founded by pirates from Cuma, the Chalcidian town in the country of the Opicans; afterwards, large numbers came from Chalcis and the rest of Euboea and helped to people the place, the founders being Perieres and Crataemenes from Cuma and Chalcis respectively. The Sicels first gave it the name Zancle because the place is shaped like a sickle, which the Sicels call zanclon. The original settlers were later expelled by some Samians and other Ionians who landed in Sicily fleeing from the Medes; the Samians in their turn, not long afterwards, were driven out by Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium, who colonized the town with a mixed population and changed its name to Messina, after his old country.

Himera was founded from Zancle by Euclides, Simus, and Sacon, most of those who went to the colony being Chalcidians, although they were joined by some exiles from Syracuse, defeated in a civil war and called the Myletidae. The language was a mixture of Chalcidian and Doric, but the institutions that prevailed were the Chalcidian. Acrae and Casmenae were founded by the Syracusans — Acrae seventy years after Syracuse, Casmenae nearly twenty after Acrae. Camarina was first founded by the Syracusans, close on a hundred and thirty-five years after the building of Syracuse; its founders were Daxon and Menecolus. But the Camarinaeans were expelled by force by the Syracusans for having revolted, and Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, some time later receiving their land in ransom for some Syracusan prisoners, resettled Camarina, himself acting as its founder. It was then again depopulated by Gelo, and settled once more for the third time by the Geloans.

Such is the list of the peoples, Hellenic and barbarian, inhabiting Sicily, and such the size of the island the Athenians were now bent on invading; in real truth they were ambitious to conquer the whole, although they had also the plausible design of helping their kindred and other allies on the island. They were especially incited by envoys from Egesta, who had come to Athens and called for their aid more urgently than ever. The Egestaeans had gone to war with their neighbours the Selinuntines over questions of marriage and disputed territory, and the Selinuntines had secured the alliance of the Syracusans and were pressing Egesta hard by land and sea. The Egestaeans now reminded the Athenians of the alliance made in the time of Laches, during the former Leontine war, and begged them to send a fleet to their aid. Among many other considerations they urged, as a capital argument, that if the Syracusans were allowed to go unpunished for their depopulation of Leontini, to ruin the allies still left to Athens in Sicily, and to get the whole power of the island into their hands, there was a danger that they might one day come with a large force, as Dorians, to the aid of their Dorian brethren, and as colonists to the aid of the Peloponnesians who had sent them out, and join with them in pulling down the Athenian empire. The Athenians, therefore, would do well to unite with the allies still left to them and make a stand against the Syracusans — especially as they, the Egestaeans, were prepared to furnish enough money to pay for the war. The Athenians, hearing these arguments constantly repeated in their assemblies by the Egestaeans and their supporters, voted first to send envoys to Egesta to see if there really was the money they talked of in the treasury and the temples, and at the same time to find out how the war with the Selinuntines stood.

The Athenian envoys were accordingly dispatched to Sicily. The same winter the Lacedaemonians and their allies, the Corinthians excepted, marched into Argive territory, ravaged a small part of the land, and took some yokes of oxen and carried off some corn. They also settled the Argive exiles at Orneae, leaving them a few soldiers from the rest of the army, and after making a truce for a certain period — by which neither Orneatae nor Argives were to harm each other’s territory — went home with the army. Not long afterwards the Athenians came with thirty ships and six hundred heavy infantry, and the Argives, joining them with their full force, marched out and besieged the men in Orneae for one day; but the garrison escaped by night, the besiegers having bivouacked some way off. The next day the Argives discovered it, razed Orneae to the ground, and went home; after which the Athenians went off in their ships. Meanwhile the Athenians took to Methone on the Macedonian border, by sea, some cavalry of their own and the Macedonian exiles who were at Athens, and plundered Perdiccas’ country. At this the Lacedaemonians sent to the Thracian Chalcidians, who had a truce with Athens renewed every ten days, urging them to join Perdiccas in the war, but they refused. So the winter ended, and with it ended the sixteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

Early in the spring of the following summer the Athenian envoys returned from Sicily, and the Egestaeans with them, bringing sixty talents of uncoined silver as a month’s pay for sixty ships, which they were going to ask to have sent. The Athenians held an assembly, and after hearing from the Egestaeans and their own envoys a report — as attractive as it was untrue — about the state of affairs generally and in particular about the money, of which it was said there was abundance in the temples and the treasury, voted to send sixty ships to Sicily under the command of Alcibiades, son of Clinias, Nicias, son of Niceratus, and Lamachus, son of Xenophanes, who were appointed with full powers. They were to help the Egestaeans against the Selinuntines, to restore Leontini if they gained any advantage in the war, and to settle all other matters in Sicily as they should think best for the interests of Athens. Five days later a second assembly was held to consider the quickest means of equipping the ships, and to vote whatever else might be required by the generals for the expedition. Nicias, who had been chosen to the command against his will, and who thought the state was ill-advised, and on a slight and specious pretext was aspiring to the conquest of all Sicily — a great matter to achieve — came forward in the hope of diverting the Athenians from the enterprise, and gave them the following counsel:

“Although this assembly was called to consider the preparations for sailing to Sicily, I think we still have this question to examine: whether it is better to send the ships at all. We ought not to give so little consideration to a matter of such weight, or let ourselves be persuaded by foreigners into a war we have nothing to do with. And yet, individually, I gain in honour by such a course, and fear as little as the next man for my person — not that I think a man any the worse citizen for taking some thought for his person and his estate; on the contrary, such a man would, for his own sake, want the prosperity of his country more than others. Still, since I have never spoken against my convictions to gain honour, I shall not begin to do so now, but will say what I think best. Against your character any words of mine would be feeble enough, if I were to advise you to keep what you have got and not risk what is actually yours for advantages which are doubtful in themselves and which you may or may not attain. I will, therefore, content myself with showing that your eagerness is out of season, and that your ambition is not easy to accomplish.

“I say, then, that you are leaving many enemies behind you here, only to go yonder and bring more back with you. You imagine, perhaps, that the treaty you have made can be relied on; a treaty that will continue to exist nominally as long as you keep quiet — for nominal it has become, owing to the practices of certain men here and at Sparta — but which, in the event of a serious reverse on any quarter, would not delay our enemies a moment in attacking us. First, because the convention was forced upon them by disaster and was less honourable to them than to us; and second, because in this very convention there are many points still in dispute. Again, some of the most powerful states have not yet accepted the arrangement at all. Some of these are at open war with us; others (as the Lacedaemonians do not yet move) are restrained by truces renewed every ten days. It is only too likely that, if they found our power divided — as we are hurrying to divide it — they would attack us vigorously together with the Siceliots, whose alliance they would have valued in the past as much as they have valued few. A man ought, therefore, to consider these points, and not think of running risks with a country in such a delicate position, or of grasping at another empire before we have secured the one we already have. The Thracian Chalcidians, in fact, have been all these years in revolt from us without yet being subdued; and others on the mainland yield us only a doubtful obedience. Meanwhile the Egestaeans, our allies, have been wronged, and we run to help them; while the rebels who have wronged us so long still wait for punishment.

“Yet the latter, if brought under, might be kept under, while the Sicilians, even if conquered, are too far off and too numerous to be ruled without difficulty. It is folly to march against men who, even if conquered, could not be held; while failure would leave us in a very different position from the one we held before the enterprise. The Siceliots, again, taking them as they are at present — in the event of a Syracusan conquest, the favourite bugbear of the Egestaeans — would, in my view, be even less dangerous to us than they are now. At present they might possibly come here as separate states for love of Lacedaemon; in the other case one empire would scarcely attack another, since after joining the Peloponnesians to overthrow ours, they could only expect to see the same hands overthrow their own in the same way. The Hellenes in Sicily would fear us most if we never went there at all, and next to that, if after displaying our power we went away again as soon as possible. We all know that what is farthest off, and the reputation of which can least be tested, is what people admire; at the least reverse they would at once begin to look down on us, and would join our enemies here against us. You have yourselves had this experience with regard to the Lacedaemonians and their allies, whom your unexpected success — compared with what you feared at first — has made you suddenly despise, tempting you on to aspire to the conquest of Sicily. Instead, however, of being puffed up by the misfortunes of your adversaries, you ought to think of breaking their spirit before giving way to confidence, and to understand that the one thought their disgrace has awakened in the Lacedaemonians is how they may even now, if possible, overthrow us and repair their dishonour, since military reputation is their oldest and chief study. Our struggle, therefore, if we are wise, will not be for the barbarian Egestaeans in Sicily, but how to defend ourselves most effectively against the oligarchical machinations of Lacedaemon.

“We should also remember that we are now only just enjoying some respite from a great pestilence and from war, to no small benefit of our estates and persons; and that it is right to use these at home for ourselves, instead of using them on behalf of these exiles, whose interest it is to lie as smoothly as they can, who do nothing but talk themselves and leave the danger to others, and who, if they succeed, will show no proper gratitude, and if they fail, will drag down their friends with them. And if there is any man here, overjoyed at being chosen to command, who urges you to make the expedition merely for ends of his own — especially if he is too young to command — who seeks to be admired for his stable of horses, but, because of its heavy expenses, hopes to make some profit from his appointment, do not allow such a one to maintain his private splendour at his country’s risk. Remember that such people damage the public fortune while they squander their own, and that this is a matter of importance, and not for a young man to decide or hastily take in hand.

“When I see such people now sitting here at the side of that same individual and summoned by him, alarm seizes me; and I in my turn summon any of the older men who may have such a person sitting next to him not to let himself be shamed down, for fear of being thought a coward if he does not vote for war, but, remembering how rarely success is got by wishing and how often by foresight, to leave to them the mad dream of conquest, and as a true lover of his country — now threatened by the greatest danger in its history — to hold up his hand on the other side; to vote that the Siceliots be left within the limits now existing between us, limits no one can complain of (the Ionian sea for the coasting voyage, and the Sicilian across the open sea), to enjoy their own possessions and settle their own quarrels; that the Egestaeans, for their part, be told to end by themselves, with the Selinuntines, the war they began without consulting the Athenians; and that for the future we do not enter into alliance, as we have been used to do, with people whom we must help in their need, and who can never help us in ours.

“And you, Prytanis, if you think it your duty to care for the commonwealth, and if you wish to show yourself a good citizen, put the question to the vote and take the opinion of the Athenians a second time. If you are afraid to move the question again, consider that a violation of the law cannot carry any prejudice with so many supporters; that you will be the physician of your misguided city; and that the virtue of men in office is briefly this — to do their country as much good as they can, or, in any case, no harm they can avoid.”

Such were the words of Nicias. Most of the Athenians who came forward spoke in favour of the expedition, and against annulling what had been voted, although some spoke on the other side. By far the warmest advocate of the expedition, however, was Alcibiades, son of Clinias, who wished to thwart Nicias both as his political opponent and because of the attack made on him in his speech, and who was, besides, exceedingly ambitious for a command by which he hoped to reduce Sicily and Carthage, and personally to gain in wealth and reputation through his successes. The position he held among the citizens led him to indulge his tastes beyond what his real means could bear, both in keeping horses and in his other expenditure; and this had not a little to do with the eventual ruin of the Athenian state. Alarmed at the greatness of his licence in his own life and habits, and of the ambition he showed in everything he undertook, the mass of the people set him down as a pretender to tyranny and became his enemies. Although his conduct of the war as a public man was as good as could be desired, his private habits gave offence to everyone, and led them to commit affairs to other hands, and so before long to ruin the city. Meanwhile he now came forward and gave the following advice to the Athenians:

“Athenians, I have a better right to command than others — I must begin with this, since Nicias has attacked me — and at the same time I believe myself worthy of it. The things for which I am abused bring fame to my ancestors and to me, and profit to my country besides. The Hellenes, after expecting to see our city ruined by the war, concluded it to be even greater than it really is, because of the magnificence with which I represented it at the Olympic games, when I sent into the lists seven chariots — a number never before entered by any private person — and won the first prize, and was second and fourth, and made sure to have everything else in a style worthy of my victory. Custom regards such displays as honourable, and they cannot be made without leaving behind them an impression of power. Again, any splendour I may have shown at home in providing choruses or otherwise, is naturally envied by my fellow citizens, but to foreigners has the look of strength, just as in the previous case. And this is no useless folly, when a man at his own private cost benefits not only himself but his city; nor is it unfair that he who prides himself on his position should refuse to be on a level with the rest. The man who is badly off has his misfortunes all to himself; and as we do not see men courted in adversity, on the same principle a man should accept the insolence of prosperity — or else, let him first measure out equal treatment to all, and then demand it for himself in turn. What I know is that men of this kind, and all others who have attained to any distinction, although they may be unpopular in their lifetime in their relations with their fellow-men, and especially with their equals, leave to posterity a desire to claim connection with them even where there is no ground for it, and are vaunted by the country to which they belonged not as strangers or wrongdoers, but as fellow-countrymen and heroes. Such are my aspirations; and however I am abused for them in private, the question is whether anyone manages public affairs better than I do. Having united the most powerful states of the Peloponnese, without great danger or expense to you, I forced the Lacedaemonians to stake their all on the issue of a single day at Mantinea; and although they won the battle, they have never since fully recovered their confidence.

“Thus did my youth and so-called monstrous folly find fitting arguments to deal with the power of the Peloponnesians, and by its ardour win their confidence and prevail. And do not be afraid of my youth now, but while I am still in its flower, and Nicias appears fortunate, make the most of the services of us both. Do not rescind your resolution to sail to Sicily on the ground that you would be going against a great power. The cities in Sicily are peopled by mixed rabbles and easily change their institutions and adopt new ones in their place; consequently, the inhabitants, having no real feeling of patriotism, are not provided with arms for their persons or properly settled on the land. Every man thinks that either by fair words or by party strife he can secure something at the public expense, and then, in the event of a catastrophe, settle in some other country, and makes his preparations accordingly. From a mob like this you need not look for either unanimity in counsel or concert in action; rather they will probably come over one by one as they get a fair offer, especially if they are torn by civil strife, as we are told. Moreover, the Siceliots have not so many heavy infantry as they boast — just as the Hellenes generally proved less numerous than each state reckoned itself to be, but Hellas greatly overestimated their numbers, and has hardly had an adequate force of heavy infantry throughout this war. The states in Sicily, therefore, from all I can hear, will be found as I say. And I have not even pointed out all our advantages, since we shall have the help of many barbarians, who from their hatred of the Syracusans will join us in attacking them. Nor will the powers at home prove any hindrance, if you judge rightly. Our fathers, with these very adversaries that we are told we shall now leave behind us when we sail, and the Mede as their enemy as well, were able to win the empire, depending solely on their superiority at sea. The Peloponnesians have never had so little hope against us as at present; and however confident they may be, although strong enough to invade our country even if we stay at home, they can never hurt us with their navy, since we leave one of our own behind us that is a match for them.

“In this state of things, what reason can we give ourselves for holding back, or what excuse can we offer to our allies in Sicily for not helping them? They are our confederates, and we are bound to assist them, without objecting that they have not assisted us. We did not take them into alliance to have them help us in Hellas, but so that they might harass our enemies in Sicily and prevent them from coming over here and attacking us. This is how empire has been won, both by us and by all others who have held it: by a constant readiness to support all, whether barbarians or Hellenes, who invite assistance. If everyone were to keep quiet or pick and choose whom they ought to assist, we should make few new conquests and would put at risk those we have already won. Men do not rest content with parrying the attacks of a superior; they often strike the first blow to prevent the attack from being made. We cannot fix the exact point at which our empire shall stop. We have reached a position in which we must not be content with retaining what we have, but must scheme to extend it; for, if we cease to rule others, we are in danger of being ruled ourselves. Nor can you look at inaction in the same light as others, unless you are also prepared to change your habits and make them like theirs.

“Be convinced, then, that we shall augment our power at home by this adventure abroad. Let us make the expedition, and so humble the pride of the Peloponnesians by sailing off to Sicily and showing them how little we care for the peace we are now enjoying; and at the same time we shall either become masters, as we very easily may, of the whole of Hellas through the addition of the Sicilian Hellenes, or in any case we shall ruin the Syracusans, to the great advantage of ourselves and our allies. The ability to stay if successful, or to return, will be guaranteed by our navy, since we shall be superior at sea to all the Siceliots put together. Do not let the do-nothing policy that Nicias advocates, or his setting of the young against the old, turn you from your purpose; but in the good old fashion in which our fathers, old and young together, by their united counsels brought our affairs to their present height, you must endeavour still to advance them. Understand that neither youth nor old age can do anything without the other; that levity, sobriety, and deliberate judgement are strongest when united; and that, by sinking into inaction, the city, like everything else, will wear itself out, and its skill in everything will decay. Each fresh struggle will give it fresh experience, and make it more accustomed to defend itself, not in word but in deed. In short, my conviction is that a city not inactive by nature could not choose a quicker way to ruin itself than by suddenly adopting such a policy, and that the safest rule of life is to take one’s character and institutions for better or for worse, and to live up to them as closely as one can.”

Such were the words of Alcibiades. After hearing him and the Egestaeans and some Leontine exiles, who came forward reminding them of their oaths and imploring their assistance, the Athenians grew more eager for the expedition than before. Nicias, seeing that it would now be useless to try to deter them with the old line of argument, but thinking he might perhaps change their minds by the extravagance of his estimates, came forward a second time and spoke as follows:

“I see, Athenians, that you are thoroughly bent on the expedition; so I hope it will turn out as we wish, and will give you my opinion at the present juncture. From all that I hear, we are going against cities that are great, and not subject to one another, or in need of change such that they would be glad to pass from enforced servitude to an easier condition, or in any way likely to accept our rule in exchange for freedom. To take only the Hellenic towns, they are very numerous for one island. Besides Naxos and Catana, which I expect to join us because of their connection with Leontini, there are seven others armed at all points just like our own — particularly Selinus and Syracuse, the chief objects of our expedition. These are full of heavy infantry, archers, and darters; they have galleys in abundance and crowds to man them. They have money too, partly in private hands, partly in the temples at Selinus, and at Syracuse first-fruits from some of the barbarians as well. But their chief advantage over us lies in the number of their horses, and in the fact that they grow their corn at home instead of importing it.

“Against a power of this kind a weak naval armament alone will not do; we shall also need a large land army to sail with us, if we are to do anything worthy of our ambition and not be shut out from the country by their numerous cavalry — especially if the cities should take alarm and combine, and we should be left without friends, except the Egestaeans, to provide us with horse to defend ourselves. It would be disgraceful to be forced to retire, or to send back for reinforcements, owing to want of forethought at the start. We must therefore start from home with an adequate force, since we are going to sail far from our country, and on an expedition unlike any we have undertaken before in the role of allies, among our subject states here in Hellas, where any additional supplies needed were easily drawn from friendly territory. We are cutting ourselves off and going to a land entirely strange, from which during four months in winter it is not even easy for a messenger to get to Athens.

“I think, therefore, that we ought to take great numbers of heavy infantry, both from Athens and from our allies, not merely from our subjects but also any we can get for love or for money in the Peloponnese, along with great numbers of archers and slingers, to face the Sicilian horse. Meanwhile we must have an overwhelming superiority at sea, to make it easier to bring in what we need; and we must take our own corn in merchant ships — wheat and parched barley — and bakers from the mills compelled to serve for pay in the proper proportion. That way, if we are ever weather-bound, the force will not run short of provisions, since not every city will be able to entertain numbers like ours. We must also provide ourselves with everything else we can, so as not to be dependent on others; and above all we must take with us from home as much money as possible, since the sums talked of as ready at Egesta are readier, you may be sure, in talk than in any other way.

“Indeed, even if we leave Athens with a force not only equal to that of the enemy except in the number of heavy infantry in the field, but even at all points superior to it, we shall still find it difficult to conquer Sicily or to save ourselves. We must not deceive ourselves: we are going to found a city among strangers and enemies, and the man who undertakes such an enterprise should be prepared to become master of the country the very day he lands, or, failing that, to find everything hostile to him. Fearing this, and knowing that we shall need much good counsel and still more good fortune — a hard thing for mortal man to count on — I want, as far as possible, to make myself independent of fortune before sailing, and when I do sail, to be as safe as a strong force can make me. This I believe to be surest for the country at large, and safest for those of us who are to go on the expedition. If anyone thinks differently, I resign my command to him.”

With this Nicias concluded, thinking he would either disgust the Athenians with the magnitude of the undertaking, or, if forced to sail, do so in the safest way possible. The Athenians, however, far from having their taste for the voyage spoiled by the burden of preparations, became more eager for it than ever; and the very opposite happened of what Nicias had thought, since it was held that he had given good advice and that the expedition would be the safest in the world. All alike fell in love with the enterprise. The older men thought they would either subdue the places against which they were sailing, or, at the very least, with such a large force, suffer no disaster. Those in the prime of life felt a longing for foreign sights and spectacles, and had no doubt they would come safely home again; while the idea of the common people and the soldiery was to earn wages on the spot and make conquests that would supply a never-ending fund of pay for the future. With this enthusiasm of the majority, the few who did not like it feared to appear unpatriotic by holding up their hands against it, and so kept quiet.

At last one of the Athenians came forward and called on Nicias and told him he ought not to make excuses or put them off, but to say at once before them all what forces the Athenians should vote him. At this he said, not without reluctance, that he would consult on the matter more at leisure with his colleagues; as far, however, as he could see at present, they must sail with at least one hundred galleys — the Athenians providing as many transports as they thought fit, and sending for others from the allies — not less than five thousand heavy infantry in all, Athenian and allied, and if possible more; and the rest of the force in proportion: archers from home and from Crete, and slingers, and whatever else seemed desirable, prepared by the generals and taken with them.

On hearing this the Athenians at once voted that the generals should have full powers in the matter of the size of the army and of the expedition generally, to do as they judged best for the interests of Athens. After this the preparations began; messages were sent to the allies and rolls drawn up at home. Since the city had just recovered from the plague and the long war, and a number of young men had grown up and capital had accumulated by reason of the truce, everything was the more easily provided.

In the midst of these preparations, all the stone Hermae in the city of Athens — the customary square figures, so common in the doorways of private houses and of temples — had, in one night, most of them their faces mutilated. No one knew who had done it, but large public rewards were offered for finding the authors; and it was further voted that anyone who knew of any other act of impiety committed should come forward and inform without fear of consequences, whether citizen, alien, or slave. The matter was taken up all the more seriously since it was thought to be ominous for the expedition, and part of a conspiracy to bring about a revolution and to overthrow the democracy.

Information was given accordingly by some resident aliens and body servants — not about the Hermae, but about some previous mutilations of other images carried out by young men in a drunken frolic, and of mock celebrations of the Mysteries said to take place in private houses. Alcibiades being implicated in this charge, it was seized on by those who could least endure him, because he stood in the way of their having undisturbed direction of the people, and who thought that if he were once removed, the first place would be theirs. They accordingly magnified the matter and loudly proclaimed that the affair of the Mysteries and the mutilation of the Hermae were part and parcel of a scheme to overthrow the democracy, and that none of it had been done without Alcibiades; the proofs alleged being the general and undemocratic licence of his life and habits.

Alcibiades on the spot rebutted the charges in question, and also, before going on the expedition — the preparations for which were now complete — offered to stand his trial, so that it could be seen whether he was guilty of the acts imputed to him; he was willing to be punished if found guilty, but, if acquitted, to take the command. Meanwhile he protested against their entertaining slanders against him in his absence, and begged them rather to put him to death at once if he were guilty, and pointed out the imprudence of sending him out at the head of so large an army with so serious a charge still undecided. But his enemies feared he would have the army on his side if he were tried immediately, and that the people might relent in favour of the man whom they already caressed as the cause of the Argives and some of the Mantineans joining the expedition; and they did their utmost to get this proposal rejected, putting forward other orators who said that he ought now to sail and not delay the departure of the army, and be tried on his return within a fixed number of days. Their plan was to have him sent for and brought home for trial on some graver charge, which they could the more easily get up in his absence. Accordingly it was decreed that he should sail.

After this the departure for Sicily took place, it being now about midsummer. Most of the allies, with the corn transports and the smaller craft and the rest of the expedition, had already received orders to muster at Corcyra, and from there to cross the Ionian Sea in a body to the Iapygian promontory. But the Athenians themselves, and such of their allies as happened to be with them, went down to Piraeus on a fixed day at daybreak, and began to man the ships for putting out to sea. With them went down also, one may say, the whole population of the city, citizens and foreigners alike — the inhabitants of the country each escorting those who belonged to them, their friends, their relatives, or their sons, with hope and lamentation as they went, thinking of the conquests they hoped to make, or of the friends they might never see again, given the long voyage they were about to make from their country. Indeed, at this moment, when they were about to part from one another, the danger came home to them more than when they had voted for the expedition; although the strength of the force, and the lavish provision they noticed in every department, was a sight that could not but comfort them. As for the foreigners and the rest of the crowd, they simply went to see a sight worth looking at, and beyond all belief.

Indeed, this force that first sailed out was by far the most costly and splendid Hellenic force ever sent out by a single city up to that time. In mere number of ships and heavy infantry, the one against Epidaurus under Pericles, and the same again when going against Potidæa under Hagnon, was not inferior, since it contained four thousand Athenian heavy infantry, three hundred horse, and a hundred galleys, accompanied by fifty Lesbian and Chian ships and many allies besides. But these were sent on a short voyage and with scanty equipment. The present expedition was formed in view of a long term of service by land and sea alike, and was furnished with ships and troops so as to be ready for either as required. The fleet had been elaborately equipped at great cost to the captains and the state: the treasury gave a drachma a day to each seaman and provided empty ships — sixty men-of-war and forty transports — manning these with the best crews obtainable; while the captains gave a bounty in addition to the treasury pay to the thranitae and crews generally, besides spending lavishly on figureheads and equipment, every one of them making the utmost effort to make his own ship excel in beauty and speed. Meanwhile the land forces had been picked from the best muster-rolls, and they vied with one another in paying close attention to their arms and personal equipment. The result was not only a rivalry among themselves in their different departments, but also an impression among the rest of the Hellenes that it was more a display of power and resources than an armament against an enemy. For if anyone had counted up the public expenditure of the state, and the private outlay of individuals — that is, the sums the state had already spent on the expedition and was sending out in the hands of the generals, and what individuals had spent on their personal outfit, or as captains of galleys had laid out and were still to lay out on their vessels — and if to this had been added the journey money each was likely to have provided himself with, independently of the pay from the treasury, for a voyage of such length, and what the soldiers or traders took with them for the purpose of trade — it would have been found that many talents in all were being taken out of the city. The expedition became famous not less for its astonishing boldness and for the splendour of its appearance than for its overwhelming strength compared with the peoples it was directed against, and for the fact that this was the longest passage from home so far attempted, and the most ambitious in its objectives considering the resources of those undertaking it.

The ships now manned, and everything they meant to sail with put on board, the trumpet commanded silence, and the prayers customary before putting out to sea were offered — not in each ship by itself, but by all together to the voice of a herald. Bowls of wine were mixed throughout the force, and libations made by the soldiers and their officers in gold and silver goblets. The crowds on shore joined in the prayers — citizens and all others who wished them well. The hymn sung and the libations finished, they put out to sea, and at first sailed out in column, then raced one another as far as Aegina, and so hurried on to reach Corcyra, where the rest of the allied forces were also assembling.
